The host association is ambiguous: the nearest LS DR10 galaxy candidate ($r_{\rm AB}\sim24.7$) is offset by $\sim4\ensuremath{''}$ ($\sim34$ kpc) with chance-alignment probability $P_{\rm cc}\sim0.2$, and current imaging does not exclude a fainter, near-coincident host.

Bayesian model comparison prefers the refreshed two-component model over the single-component top-hat fit (Table [\[tab:pri_post\]](#tab:pri_post)), supporting the interpretation that additional dynamical structure (energy injection and/or angular stratification) is a required feature of this GRB afterglow.

GRB 250818B is only the third short GRB to have a detected radio afterglow at $z > 1$, with the other two short GRBs being GRB 170728B (cite: 2022ApJ...940...56F) and GRB 210726A (cite: 2024ApJ...970..139S).

Because these scenarios imply very different physical offsets (and therefore limit the use of offset-based arguments), we place particular emphasis on constraints that arise directly from the broadband afterglow data.
In particular, when prompt-emission constraints are weak or unavailable, the afterglow becomes the primary handle on the explosion energetics and environment.
To reduce the strong $\beta$–$A_V$ degeneracy inherent to three-band photometry, we incorporate an X-ray-informed prior on $\beta$.

A single-component top-hat jet provides a reasonable overall fit but does not reproduce the full evolution: it exhibits a noticeable mismatch to the X-ray light curve from $\sim 0.02$ d, underpredicts the optical emission at $\gtrsim 3$ d, and underpredicts the 36.8 GHz detection at $\sim 4$ – $5$ d (noting the large uncertainty on this point).

The absorbed power-law model provides an adequate description of the data (CSTAT/DoF = 0.24), with no systematic residuals; given the limited photon statistics, we therefore do not explore more complex spectral models.
